lesson_a.title: Do You Have to See It to Know It?

objectives.text: Distinguish how you know something, what your evidence establishes, and when a report needs further checking.

challenge.text: Notice three things you know today. Identify how you know each and the limits of what you can say.

check_in.text: Can you now explain how you know something and what your evidence does not establish?

situation.text: Imagine your grandmother calls from the village and says the apricot tree you planted has fruit.
You are far away. She stands beside the tree, looking at its branches.

question.text: Must you see it yourself before you can know that it has fruit?

visual.alt: A faceless grandmother beside an apricot tree with a phone.

prompt.text: Can you know something you have not seen with your own eyes?

spans.text: Yes, depending on the evidence.
I need to see it myself.
I have not decided.

reveal.text: Keep your answer in mind and examine three situations before returning to it.

visual.alt: A closed box with a blank label at a house door.

spans.text: Imagine stepping outside and finding a closed box at your door, with a label bearing your name.
What you observed was the box and label. You did not see anyone bring it.
In this ordinary situation, the parcel strongly supports the conclusion that someone brought it.
It may reasonably be your expected order, but the label alone does not reveal its contents.
The evidence identifies neither the person who brought it nor its arrival time. Those are separate questions.

prompt.text: Which statement separates observation from inference?

spans.text: I saw a delivery worker place it, because the box is there.
I observed a box and inferred that someone brought it.
I saw the contents from my name on the label.

title.text: An open book and warm tea

visual.alt: A library table with an open book and gently steaming tea.

spans.text: Imagine a table in a quiet library, with an open book and a cup of tea.
You touch the cup and feel its warmth. You see nobody at the table.
The cup’s warmth is a direct observation. Someone having been here recently is a reasonable inference, not an observation.
The tea might be kept warm another way, so the cup alone cannot establish when someone left.

prompt.text: Which wording best fits these traces?

spans.text: The reader left exactly two minutes ago.
Nothing can be inferred.
Someone was probably here recently, without knowing who.
Direct observation includes more than sight. You sense the cup’s warmth through touch.
Inference connects a trace with an explanation while keeping reasonable alternatives in view.
Your grandmother’s report is a third route, if she is truthful and actually looking at the tree.
There are two different questions about a source: are they truthful, and are they placed to know?

prompt.text: Classify the route of knowledge, rather than its subject.

spans.text: You taste a piece and sense its sweetness.
You smell coffee from a nearby cup.
You see a parcel and infer that someone brought it.
Your truthful grandmother reports what she sees on the tree.
From warm tea, you infer that someone was probably here recently.
Imagine a traveller who needs the last bus to get home.
A nearby passenger confidently says it was cancelled. The traveller begins looking for another way home.

visual.alt: Two faceless passengers beside a bus at a night station.

spans.text: The traveller asks how the passenger knows, and learns that he overheard another passenger.
The passenger cannot see the departure system and has not asked station staff.

visual.alt: Two passengers near a bus, with a ticket window behind them.

spans.text: The traveller goes to the ticket window before changing plans.
The clerk checks the current operating record and confirms that the bus is delayed but still running.

visual.alt: A traveller and a lit ticket window with a clerk and text-free screen.

spans.text: The traveller waits near the platform, having distinguished someone repeating a report from someone who checked it.

visual.alt: A bus beside the station platform and ticket window.

prompt.text: Why was the clerk’s answer stronger here?

spans.text: He checked the current operating record available to him.
The latest report is always right.
The passenger must have been lying.

prompt.text: Which report would you check more carefully?

spans.text: A neighbour who uses the bakery tells you its opening time.
A stranger says the tap water is unsafe today.
I would check both equally.

reveal.text: Consider the source’s access, the stakes of the decision, and whether the report is unusual.

spans.text: An ordinary report from someone truthful and placed to know may be enough for a simple decision.
As the consequences grow, you need clearer evidence. Confidence in a voice is not verification.
For the water report, look for a notice from the relevant local authority instead of relying on an anonymous warning.
Asking for verification does not accuse the speaker of lying. They may be honest but uninformed.

prompt.text: What is the best way to evaluate this clip?

spans.text: Believe it because he speaks confidently.
Check the source’s identity and evidence, and consult a qualified professional before a health decision.
Reject every report from one person.

situation.text: Imagine a clip of an unnamed man claiming that a herbal drink can replace diabetes medication.

spans.text: Ask whether you sensed this yourself, inferred it, or received a report.
Separate a trace from its interpretation, and choose wording that matches your evidence.
Check the source’s truthfulness and access, and investigate more carefully when the stakes grow.

objectives.text: Distinguish nothing at all from an empty place, and examine why nothing alone cannot explain something’s existence.

challenge.text: Notice “nothing” in ordinary conversation. Ask whether it means a particular absence or the absence of everything.

check_in.text: Can you distinguish a particular absence from nothing, without treating an unknown cause as an absent cause?

situation.text: Imagine a museum guard checking a glass display case after closing.
The case contains no exhibits. In the morning, the guard sees a vase inside.

question.text: Does “it was empty” mean the vase came from nothing?

visual.alt: An empty glass case on a pedestal in a night museum, with a faceless guard.

prompt.text: What would you ask first?

spans.text: Who could access the case?
Did nothing make the vase?
Was my observation complete?

reveal.text: Start with what you actually saw, then examine an explanation for what changed.

spans.text: The guard wants to protect the exhibits, so he reviews his closing notes.
He recorded that the case was empty, but did not watch it all night.

visual.alt: A guard beside a glass case in a quiet museum.

spans.text: He neither accuses anyone nor treats his missing explanation as the vase’s cause.
He asks the curator about the key and the exhibit transfer record.

visual.alt: A vase inside the display case, with a guard nearby.

spans.text: The curator shows a record of the vase’s transfer after he left, and explains that she opened and closed the case.

visual.alt: A display case and gold vase under museum lighting.

spans.text: The guard updates his note: he saw an empty case, but did not see what happened afterward.
He reached an explanation by investigating something that could account for the change.

visual.alt: A vase resting inside a closed glass case.

prompt.text: What is wrong with “I did not see who placed the vase, so it came from nothing”?

spans.text: Everything I do not see is absent.
Not knowing the cause does not establish that every cause is absent.
The guard must be blamed.
In the scenario, the case, glass, key, and guard still existed even when no vase was inside.
Here, “empty” means no exhibit inside, rather than the absence of everything.
In our question, nothing means no thing exists: no place, materials, or working power.
If you imagine a dark space waiting for something, you have imagined a place, not nothing.
Black in an illustration is only a background. A picture cannot display the absence of everything.

prompt.text: Which describes the absence of a particular thing, and which means nothing at all?

categories.label: Nothing at all in the question

spans.text: A case without exhibits.
A kitchen without ready bread.
No place, material, or anything exists.
A room with its furniture removed.

visual.alt: A bakery kitchen with a flour sack, bowl, oven, and faceless baker.

spans.text: Imagine a baker wanting to make a loaf, with no ready bread in the kitchen.
In this example, the baker prepares flour and water, shapes dough, and uses the oven.
The loaf’s absence at the start does not mean the things used to make it are absent.
The loaf did not appear from nothing. Existing things were changed through the baker’s work.
This illustrates the distinction. It does not make the universe a loaf or a Creator a baker who needs ingredients.

prompt.text: Which part assigns nothing a property excluded by its definition?

spans.text: By nothing, I mean the absence of everything.
There is no material or power in it.
But it can wait and then produce material.

prompt.text: Does “I do not know how it happened” answer “why did it happen”?

spans.text: It acknowledges my limited knowledge.
I might see it as a provisional answer.
I need to think more.

reveal.text: You can stop at “I do not know” while keeping the question open. You need not fill the gap with a misleading label.

spans.text: If nothing means the absence of everything, it supplies nothing that explains a new existence.
This examines “nothing produced something.” It does not turn a difficult question into an account of the universe’s history.
We have not established that the universe began, or how it began. Establishing that requires further evidence.
Excluding an explanation does not automatically establish every detail of another explanation.
The remaining question is: if existence needs an explanation, what could do that job?

prompt.text: Judge the understanding, then choose the reason.

statement.text: “I did not see a cause” means “it is established that no cause exists.”

spans.text: Observation covers everything that could happen.
Missing knowledge is insufficient evidence that a cause is absent.
Every hidden thing must be believed.
Distinguish an empty place from the absence of everything.
Do not give nothing materials or power and still call it nothing.
Say “I do not know the cause” when you do not. Then examine explanations without jumping to a conclusion.

objectives.text: Distinguish an existing thing changing from bringing itself into existence, and identify the problem in “it created itself.”

challenge.text: When you hear “it made itself,” identify whether it means change in something existing or self-creation before existence.

check_in.text: Can you explain the difference between changing something existing and asking something absent to create itself?

situation.text: Imagine a carpenter showing a visitor a finished chair, with boards and tools beside it.

question.text: If the chair does not yet exist, can it make itself?

visual.alt: A workshop with a chair, boards, tools, and a faceless carpenter.

prompt.text: What might “it made itself” mean?

spans.text: Something already existing changed.
It brought itself into existence before existing.
The phrase is unclear to me.

reveal.text: We will separate the meanings. The wording may hide two different ideas.

spans.text: A visitor wants to understand how the chair appeared, rather than how it looks now.
Seeing the carpenter repair a joint, he imagines the chair assembling itself in the same way.

visual.alt: A finished chair and carpenter near a workbench.

spans.text: The carpenter asks him to picture the time before the chair existed: boards and tools, but no chair.

visual.alt: Boards in a workshop, with a faint chair behind them.

spans.text: The visitor tries to picture the chair picking up a tool, then stops: the supposed chair does not yet exist.

visual.alt: A faint chair position and nearby carpentry tools.

spans.text: He changes his question: how did the boards become a chair?
He now has a question about existing things and work, rather than asking a nonexistent chair to make itself.

visual.alt: A quiet workshop with a chair, boards, and workbench.

prompt.text: Which step assumes the thing it is trying to explain?

spans.text: This chair did not exist.
The chair picked up a tool to make itself.
Then it existed after its own work.

visual.alt: A chair, tools, and boards in a lit workshop.

spans.text: For something to act, it cannot be entirely absent when that action occurs.
If it brought itself into existence, we would need it as an agent before it existed.
That makes the same thing “existing to act” and “not yet existing” at the same time.
“It made itself very quickly” does not solve this. Speed does not make a nonexistent thing an agent.
We are examining self-creation, not claiming that every change needs a human carpenter.

prompt.text: Judge the statement, then choose the reason.

statement.text: “It made itself” poses no problem if it happened quickly.

spans.text: Speed removes the need for an agent to exist.
Tools always exist.
A fast action still requires something existing to be its agent.

title.text: Did it change, or create itself?

visual.alt: Soil, a seed, a sprout, a faceless gardener, and a watering can.

spans.text: Imagine a planted seed watered by a gardener, with a plant later emerging from it.
In this situation, we began with an existing seed and surrounding conditions, rather than the absence of everything.
Describing change does not make the seed an agent before it existed.
“The plant grew” differs from “the plant brought itself into existence while absent.”
The gardener belongs to the scenario. The example does not establish that every instance of growth needs human intervention.

prompt.text: Classify the intended meaning, rather than merely noticing something new.

spans.text: A carpenter repairs a joint in an existing chair.
A nonexistent chair holds a tool to make itself.
A plant emerges from an existing seed in the scenario.
Something entirely absent starts working to create itself.

prompt.text: Which question remains after this comparison?

spans.text: What explains the existence of something dependent on other things?
How did this particular change happen?
I want to examine the idea again.

reveal.text: You can leave detailed questions open. Understanding a problem in one explanation does not require accepting every alternative.

title.text: What does this establish, and what does it leave open?

spans.text: If self-creation means acting before existence, the explanation assigns the agent’s role to something absent.
A process beginning with existing material or a system is not self-creation in this sense.
Something having always existed, if true, is a different claim. It is not self-creation before existence.
The example does not make the universe a chair, or alone establish that everything in it depends on a Creator.
Excluding self-creation does not by itself determine a Creator’s attributes. The next question needs examination.

prompt.text: Which correction is most precise?

spans.text: A seed growing means it created itself before existing.
Anything new means self-creation.
Its growth in the example starts with an existing seed, not an absent seed acting.

title.text: Test the idea before its label

spans.text: First identify whether you mean change to something existing or a thing creating itself.
Ask what acts at the moment of action. Do not give an absent thing an existing thing’s role.
Keep the conclusion’s limits. Excluding an explanation does not replace examining alternatives.
